name: Marayoor Sandalwood Forests & Muniyara Dolmens
tagline: Kerala’s only natural sandalwood stands and ancient dolmen fields in a dry Ghats valley
summary: Marayoor (Marayur) is a rain‑shadow valley north of Munnar famed for Kerala’s only natural sandalwood forests, prehistoric dolmens (muniyara) and rock art; best seen in the dry season.
description: Marayoor sits on the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats in Devikulam taluk, Idukki. The area preserves natural stands of Santalum album (sandalwood), protected by the State Forest Department, and a landscape of rocky hills, sugarcane fields and scrub‑forest.

Scattered across the hills are Muniyara — dolmenoid cists and megalithic burial chambers — and several prehistoric rock‑painting shelters. These archaeological features give Marayoor a unique mix of living forest heritage and very old human traces.

Visitors combine roadside views of the sandalwood reserve and the Forest Department depot with short walks to dolmen clusters, rock‑art sites and nearby Chinnar Wildlife Sanctuary (Thoovanam trek). The dry season gives the best access, clearer views and easier treks.
highlights: Kerala’s only naturally growing sandalwood forests (Marayoor reserve).
Muniyara dolmens — prehistoric megalithic burial chambers and hilltop viewpoints.
Prehistoric rock paintings at Ezhuthupara, Attala and nearby shelters.
Marayoor sharkara (local jaggery) and sugarcane landscapes.
Gateway to Chinnar Wildlife Sanctuary and the Thoovanam falls trek.

sections.heading: Background
body: Marayoor (also spelled Marayur) is a dry, rain‑shadow valley about 40–42 km north of Munnar. The town and surrounding reserve protect a rare natural population of sandalwood trees and a rich dry‑forest ecology that contrasts with Kerala’s wetter Western Ghats slopes.

Archaeological remains — dolmenoid cists called muniyara and rock paintings — show human presence and funerary practices from the Stone Age and later megalithic periods. These sites are protected and form part of the area’s cultural heritage.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Sandalwood reserve and forest depot: view the dark, fragrant stands from the roadside and visit the Forest Department depot that handles sandalwood processing (forest‑walks into reserves normally require prior permission).
Muniyara dolmens and rock art: short walks lead to clusters of dolmens and painted shelters (Ezhuthupara, Attala). Treat these as protected monuments — do not touch or deface the stones or paintings.

Chinnar Wildlife Sanctuary & Thoovanam trek: combine Marayoor with a guided trek to Thoovanam falls in Chinnar (Forest Department guides/fees apply). Also buy fresh Marayoor jaggery from local units during the harvest season.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Best season: the dry season gives the best access — clear trails and views. The widely recommended window is roughly September–May, with December–April the driest and most reliable months for dolmens and forest walks; avoid heavy monsoon periods for treks.

Permits & guides: walks inside the sandalwood reserve and Chinnar treks require Forest Department permission or a guide; check and book at the Munnar/Chinnar check post or the local forest office. Confirm opening times, guide availability and any ecotour fees before you travel.

latest.text: Kerala Responsible Tourism lists a 'Discover Ancient Marayoor' package that schedules visits to the sandalwood forest, dolmens and Anakottappara honeycomb rock; the package page gives current timing blocks and encourages booking through the RTMS portal.
Kerala Tourism feature (Nov 2024) highlights the Muniyara dolmens at Marayoor and recommends evening treks (around 4:00–5:30 pm) for panoramic views.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Dry season — roughly December to April (broader good window September–May).
visitorInfo.howToReach: About 40–42 km by road north of Munnar on SH‑17 (Munnar–Udumalpet). Nearest airport: Cochin/COK (~142 km); nearest major railheads: Aluva or Coimbatore. Best accessed by car/taxi; pair with a Munnar base.
etiquette: Get Forest Department permission or a licensed guide before entering sandalwood reserves or doing Chinnar treks — rules and fees change; confirm locally.
Do not touch, climb on or graffiti dolmens or rock paintings — they are protected archaeological sites.
Carry water and sturdy shoes for short rocky walks; mobile coverage can be patchy in parts of the range.
Buy jaggery from recognised local units (Marayoor sharkara has a GI tag); avoid purchasing sandalwood or wood products from uncertified sellers.
